title: Less than you think: Prevalence and predictors of fake news dissemination on Facebook
screen_reason: Behavioural Facebook profile data linked to a representative US survey panel; reports the share of respondents who posted at least one link to a fake-news domain in 2016 (8.5%), with a stated denominator (1,191 linked respondents) and a party breakdown. This is observed (not hypothetical) sharing, so it meets the SHARING criterion.

estimates.date: 2016 calendar year of Facebook timeline posts; survey waves 9 April 2016 - 7 November 2016; profile data collection began 16 November 2016
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents with linked Facebook profile data who shared at least one article from a fake news domain
estimates.value_raw: 8.5% of respondents with linked Facebook data shared at least one fake news article (Table 1: 1090/1191 = 91.5% shared none)
estimates.denominator: 1,191 US survey respondents (YouGov panel, N=3500 at wave 1) whose Facebook profile data was successfully linked
estimates.definition: Respondent posted to their own Facebook timeline at least one link whose domain appears on the BuzzFeed/Silverman list of 21 fake news domains (hard-news domains removed via the Bakshy et al. classifier)
estimates.misinfo_def: "knowingly false or misleading content created largely for the purpose of generating ad revenue"
estimates.source_quote: 8.5% of respondents for whom we have linked Facebook data
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 1-2 (with Table 1, Distribution of fake news shares)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain list assembled by journalist Craig Silverman (BuzzFeed) from BuzzSumo most-shared election domains plus follow-up reporting; 30 domains filtered with the Bakshy et al. supervised hard-news classifier down to 21 domains. Robustness list: Allcott and Gentzkow's fact-check-derived domains. No inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In particular, we used a list of fake news domains assembled by Craig Silverman of BuzzFeed News, the primary journalist covering the phenomenon as it developed (7). ... The resulting list contains 21 mostly pro-Trump domains, including well-known purveyors such as abcnews.com.co, the Denver Guardian, and Ending the Fed.
estimates.notes: Headline prevalence figure of the paper. Denominator 1,191 confirmed by Table 1 counts summing to 1,191 (1090+63+12+8+5+9+4). Value is stated verbatim in the text, not computed as a complement. Coded SHARING/actor_share per the instruction's definition ("% of users who shared any"); an adjudicator could alternatively read it as REACH with reach_subtype=sharing, since it is a behavioural at-least-once measure at the person level. Quote trimmed to the longest span that is contiguous in the two-column text rendering (the columns interleave line by line, so the sentence cannot be quoted whole). It reads in full: "According to our main measure of fake news content, 8.5% of respondents for whom we have linked Facebook data shared at least one such article to their friends."

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Table 1's "0: 1090 (91.5%)" is the exact complement of the 8.5% row and was not entered as a separate estimate. (2) Mean counts of fake news articles shared (conservatives 0.75, very conservative 1.0, over-65s 0.75, next-oldest 0.26, Republicans 0.506, independents 0.480) are per-capita intensities but exist only for demographic/ideological subgroups - no overall mean is reported - so no per_capita_intensity row was kept. (3) "3.4% of respondents ... shared 10 or fewer links of any kind", 26.1% shared 10-100 links and 61.3% shared 100-1000 links describe total link sharing, not misinformation, so they are out of scope. (4) The alternate Allcott and Gentzkow measure is used only in regression columns 3-4; no separate prevalence share is reported for it, so no definition_variant row exists. (5) Construct call to flag: 8.5% is a person-level at-least-once behavioural measure of SHARING; coded SHARING/actor_share rather than REACH/reach_subtype=sharing.

rob.design: Three-wave YouGov online panel survey of US adults (wave 1 N=3,500, 9 April-1 May 2016; wave 2 N=2,635; wave 3 N=2,628), sample-matched with YouGov weights applied. Facebook profile data solicited from 16 November 2016: 1,331 of 3,500 (38%) consented, 49.1% of the 2,711 who reported having a Facebook account, and 1,191 were successfully linked (~44% of Facebook users in the sample). Sharing measured by parsing domains of links posted to respondents' own timelines and matching against a journalist-curated 21-domain list (Silverman/BuzzFeed, hard-news domains removed with the Bakshy et al. supervised classifier), with an Allcott and Gentzkow fact-check-derived list as robustness. No inter-coder reliability statistics reported (classification is list-based). Authors note deleted posts were not observable and that consenting respondents were somewhat more liberal and more politically engaged (Table 3).
